meta.label: Crypto exchanges
meta.attribution: Compares places to buy and hold crypto in the US, UK and EU: exchanges and brokers (Coinbase, Kraken, Binance and others), crypto inside payment and investing apps (Cash App, PayPal, Robinhood, Fidelity), and three routes that are not an exchange account: a spot bitcoin ETF, self-custody in your own wallet, and not holding crypto at all. NOT FINANCIAL ADVICE. Crypto prices are extremely volatile, and crypto held on a platform is generally not covered by FDIC, SIPC or the UK's FSCS: if the platform fails or is hacked you may lose everything, as customers of the crypto lender Celsius did in 2022 (the FCA notes it owed users $4.7 billion). Method, on a 0 to 100 scale set by Conscious Consuming from the cited record. Safety and security: custody practice the platform states (cold storage, segregation, insurance, independent certifications such as SOC 2 or ISO 27001), lowered for thefts or data breaches documented by a regulator, filing or the FBI. Regulatory record: enforcement by the SEC, CFTC, US Department of Justice, CFPB and state regulators (a criminal guilty plea scores lowest; a dismissed case is not counted against a firm, and the reason given for dismissal is quoted), raised for current authorisation in ESMA's interim MiCA register of crypto-asset service providers (CASPS file, read 2026-10) and the FCA's list of registered cryptoasset firms (read 2026-10). 'No enforcement action was found in this review' means the regulators' releases searched did not show one, not that none exists. Trading fees: the cost a new small customer pays on the platform's cheapest published retail route, from its own fee page (about 0.1% scores 90, 0.4% to 0.8% scores 60 to 78, 1% scores about 60, 2% or more scores 30 or less); spreads that are not published are noted as a cost and scored down. Transparency: accountant-run or regularly updated proof of reserves, or audited accounts filed by a listed company, score highest; a self-published Merkle-tree proof scores mid-range; an old one-off review or a bare 1:1 claim scores low. Not scored: which coins are listed, staking yields, derivatives, tax reporting tools and customer service speed. A cell is left empty when the platform's page could not be read (Bitpanda's fees, OKX's security page) or the criterion does not apply to a route. Sources: SEC press and litigation releases and EDGAR filings (Coinbase 8-K, Gemini 10-K, Robinhood 10-K, eToro 20-F), DOJ, CFTC, CFPB, FBI IC3, the California Attorney General, Indiana DFI, ESMA, the FCA, SIPC, investor.gov, and each provider's own fee, security and proof-of-reserves pages. Reviewed 2026-10. Suggest changes via Contribute.

reads.text: Compare crypto exchanges by security, fees, complaint record, and disclosure.

axes.label: Fees or overall fit
axes.question: Lower fees or a stronger overall fit?

axes.label: Complaint record
axes.question: Do you want the cleaner complaint record?

consumer.axes: Round 8 practical decision dials, with the S4 cost-or-values default where evidence permits.
consumer.budget: Round 8 honest budget eligibility, with S4 refusing to guess missing cost data.
consumer.archetypes: Round 8 computed answer slots matched to available category evidence.

products.name: Coinbase
products.description: A Nasdaq-listed US exchange with a simple buy screen and a cheaper order-book mode (Coinbase Advanced). Licensed under MiCA in the EU and registered with the FCA in the UK. In May 2025 it disclosed that bribed support contractors had taken customer personal data, though not passwords, keys or funds.

security.note: Coinbase's Form 8-K of 14 May 2025 reports that a threat actor paid contractors or employees in overseas support roles to take customer data (names, addresses, masked bank and Social Security digits, ID images, balances). The filing states 'The Incident did not involve the compromise of passwords or private keys', and Coinbase said it would reimburse customers tricked into sending funds. No customer crypto was taken, but a large insider data leak lowers the score.

complaints.note: The SEC dismissed its 2023 unregistered-exchange case against Coinbase in February 2025, saying the dismissal rested on policy reform 'not on any assessment of the merits'. Coinbase Luxembourg S.A. holds a MiCA licence (ESMA interim register, authorised 20/06/2025) and CB Payments Ltd is on the FCA cryptoasset register.

fees.note: Coinbase's fee disclosure says simple buys include a spread, plus a Coinbase fee that 'may also charge a 1.875%' depending on payment method, and a 1% fee on simple limit orders. Coinbase Advanced has no spread, but its entry-tier maker and taker rates are shown only after sign-in, so the score rests on the simple-buy cost most new customers pay.

transparency.note: Coinbase says it is a public company that publishes financial statements quarterly and is audited annually by an independent third party, and that it holds customer assets 1:1. It does not publish a separate on-chain proof of reserves; the audited filings are the main evidence.

products.name: Kraken
products.description: A long-running exchange (Payward) with an app for instant buys and Kraken Pro for order-book trading. Publishes accountant-run proof of reserves, holds ISO 27001 certification, and is MiCA-licensed in Ireland and FCA-registered in the UK.

security.note: Kraken's security page says it uses cold storage and hot wallet solutions with infrastructure in guarded cages, encrypts sensitive account data at rest, is ISO/IEC 27001:2022 certified and has completed a SOC 2 Type 1 examination. No customer-fund theft is recorded in the sources read for this review.

complaints.note: The SEC filed a joint stipulation on 27 March 2025 to dismiss, with prejudice, its November 2023 case against Payward (Kraken). Payward Europe Solutions Limited is MiCA-authorised by the Central Bank of Ireland (ESMA interim register, 25/06/2025) and PAYWARD LTD. is on the FCA cryptoasset register.

fees.note: Kraken's fee schedule says it charges a 1% trading fee on instant and recurring trades (1.5% on custom orders) plus a spread; on Kraken Pro the entry tier is 0.40% maker and 0.80% taker, falling with volume or assets held.

transparency.note: Kraken's proof-of-reserves page shows a June 30, 2026 snapshot with reserve ratios such as BTC 102.9% and ETH 100.5%, and lets clients verify their own balance was included. The reviews are carried out by outside accountants, and the page lists methodology shortcomings.

products.name: Gemini
products.description: A New York trust company exchange founded by the Winklevoss twins, listed on Nasdaq since September 2025. Strong security certifications, but its Earn lending product with Genesis froze in 2022 and led to a New York regulator penalty.

security.note: Gemini's security page says it is the world's first SOC 1 Type 2 and SOC 2 Type 2 certified crypto exchange and custodian, with ISO 27001 and annual penetration testing.

complaints.note: Gemini's 2025 annual report (Form 10-K) records a February 2024 consent order with the New York Department of Financial Services: a $37.0 million civil penalty 'related primarily to the Earn program' and a $40.0 million contribution to Earn users, who later recovered their assets in kind. The SEC's 2023 Earn case reached a resolution in principle in 2025. A 2025 CFTC $5 million settlement was partly vacated in May 2026 when the CFTC said the complaint should not have been filed.

fees.note: Gemini's ActiveTrader fee schedule (1 September 2026) charges 0.600% maker and 1.200% taker at the entry tier, falling to 0.400%/0.800% from $10K monthly volume. That is high for an order book.

transparency.note: The 10-K states Gemini's Class A stock began trading on the Nasdaq Global Select Market on 12 September 2025, so it now files audited annual accounts with the SEC. No separate on-chain proof of reserves was found in the filing.

products.name: Binance
products.description: The world's largest exchange by volume, with very low trading fees. In November 2023 it pleaded guilty to US anti-money-laundering, unlicensed money transmitting and sanctions violations and agreed to pay over $4 billion. Not available to US residents (see Binance.US), and absent from the ESMA MiCA register and the FCA cryptoasset register.

security.note: Binance's proof-of-reserves page says it has 'zero debt in our capital structure' and an emergency fund (SAFU) for extreme cases such as hacks. No independent security certification or cold-storage share was shown on the pages read, so the score is middling.

complaints.note: Binance Holdings pleaded guilty in November 2023 to Bank Secrecy Act, unlicensed money transmitting and sanctions (IEEPA) violations and agreed to pay over $4 billion (DOJ). The SEC's separate civil case was dismissed with prejudice on 29 May 2025 as 'a policy matter'. As of October 2026 no Binance entity appears in ESMA's interim MiCA register of authorised providers or in the FCA's registered cryptoasset firms list.

fees.note: Binance's fee page lists 0.100% maker and 0.100% taker for regular users, 25% less when paying fees in BNB. Among the lowest entry fees in this comparison.

transparency.note: Binance publishes a self-run proof of reserves using a Merkle tree and zk-SNARK proofs so users can check their balance is counted, and claims 1:1 backing. It is not an accountant's attestation, and Binance is a private company with no published audited accounts.

products.name: Binance.US
products.description: The separate US affiliate of Binance, run by BAM Trading Services, with near-zero order-book fees. It was a co-defendant in the SEC case dismissed in 2025 and carries the parent group's history.

security.note: Binance.US says it is audited to SOC 2 Type II, ISO 27001 and ISO 27701 standards and holds the majority of user assets in US-based offline cold storage.

complaints.note: The SEC's 29 May 2025 litigation release dismissed with prejudice its case against Binance Holdings, BAM Trading Services Inc. (the Binance.US operator) and Changpeng Zhao. Binance.US says it is a FinCEN-registered money services business licensed as a money transmitter in 32 states (its own fees page). The parent group's 2023 criminal plea weighs on the score.

fees.note: Binance.US 'charges a flat 0% maker and 0.01% taker fee' on its Tier 0 pair (BNB/USD) and 0% maker / 0.02% taker on all other pairs; ACH deposits and withdrawals are free.

transparency.note: Binance.US states 'Customer reserves 1:1' and calls itself a full reserve platform, but its proof-of-reserves URL returned a not-found page in October 2026 and it publishes no audited accounts, so the claim could not be checked.

products.name: Crypto.com
products.description: A large app-first platform (Foris DAX) with a card program and a separate order-book exchange. MiCA-licensed via Malta and FCA-registered in the UK; its proof of reserves rests on a one-off December 2022 accountant review.

security.note: Crypto.com's security page describes a zero-trust, defence-in-depth approach and least-privilege access to funds, and says US customers' USD balances sit at FDIC-member banks, while warning that FDIC insurance does not cover Crypto.com's own failure, theft or fraud. No current certification list or cold-storage share was shown on the page read.

complaints.note: Foris DAX MT Limited (Crypto.com) holds a MiCA licence from the Malta Financial Services Authority (ESMA interim register, authorised 27/01/2025) and FORIS DAX UK LIMITED is on the FCA cryptoasset register. No US criminal or SEC enforcement action was found in this review.

fees.note: The Crypto.com Exchange fee table (updated 15 October 2026) charges 0.250% maker and 0.500% taker below $10,000 monthly volume, lower with volume or a CRO balance. App purchases are priced separately and usually cost more.

transparency.note: Crypto.com's proof-of-reserves page still points to a verification conducted by Mazars Group under ISRS 4400 with a Merkle tree for users to check balances. The page describes a query of customer balances 'as of December 7, 2022' and no newer accountant report was found, so the score is mid-range.

products.name: Robinhood Crypto
products.description: Crypto inside the Robinhood investing app, with no stated commission on the default route but a spread that includes a payment to Robinhood. Licensed by New York's DFS; Robinhood bought Bitstamp in 2025.

security.note: Robinhood says it holds the majority of customer coins in cold storage and carries crime insurance underwritten by Lloyd's syndicates that protects a portion of assets against theft, including cybersecurity breaches. Crypto at Robinhood Crypto is not FDIC insured or SIPC protected.

complaints.note: Robinhood Europe UAB holds a MiCA licence from the Bank of Lithuania (ESMA interim register, 29/05/2025) and Robinhood U.K. Ltd is on the FCA cryptoasset register. In September 2024 Robinhood Crypto paid a $3.9 million settlement to the California Attorney General over past limits on withdrawing crypto (see links).

fees.note: Robinhood's order-routing article says that on the default market-maker route 'for every $100 of notional crypto order volume executed through market maker routing, Robinhood Crypto receives $0.95' from its market maker, included in the spread. Exchange routing charges published fee tiers of 0.00% to 0.95%.

transparency.note: Robinhood Markets files audited annual reports with the SEC; its 2025 Form 10-K explains that the overwhelming majority of customer coins sit in cold storage in the US and EU, held in omnibus wallets for customers, and discusses customer ownership rights if the firm failed.

products.name: Bitstamp
products.description: A long-running exchange, now 'Bitstamp by Robinhood' after Robinhood bought it in June 2025. Plain order-book fees, a MiCA licence in Luxembourg and FCA registration in the UK.

security.note: Bitstamp says all customer crypto and fiat is stored separately from corporate funds, crypto is kept offline, and its custodians provide insurance for client assets held in cold wallets.

complaints.note: Bitstamp Europe S.A. holds a MiCA licence from Luxembourg's CSSF (ESMA interim register, 15/05/2025) and Bitstamp UK Limited is on the FCA cryptoasset register; Bitstamp also lists Singapore MAS and US money-services licences. No enforcement action was found in this review.

fees.note: Bitstamp's unified fee schedule (valid from 15 October 2026) charges 0.30% maker and 0.40% taker below $10,000 monthly volume, falling with volume.

transparency.note: Bitstamp says its financial controls are reviewed annually by external parties and that each year since 2016 it has been audited by a Big Four accounting firm; it does not publish an on-chain proof of reserves. Its owner Robinhood is a public company.

products.name: OKX
products.description: A large global exchange with low order-book fees and a long-running monthly proof of reserves. In February 2025 the operator pleaded guilty in the US to running an unlicensed money transmitting business; its Malta arm holds a MiCA licence.

complaints.note: Aux Cayes FinTech Co. (OKX) pleaded guilty on 24 February 2025 to one count of operating an unlicensed money transmitting business and agreed to pay more than $504 million; prosecutors said it was used for over $5 billion of suspicious transactions. OKX Europe Limited holds a MiCA licence from Malta's MFSA (ESMA interim register); no OKX entity appears on the FCA cryptoasset register.

fees.note: OKX's fee page lists 0.2000% maker and 0.3500% taker for regular users with under $100,000 in assets or monthly volume.

transparency.note: OKX's proof-of-reserves page shows its 47th report (verification date 8 September 2026, $27.4B in primary assets), with per-asset ratios such as BTC 109%, Merkle tree and zk-STARK proofs. Self-published rather than an accountant's opinion.

products.name: Uphold
products.description: A multi-asset app (crypto, stablecoins, metals) that publishes its reserves and obligations live. Easy to use but its spreads on bitcoin and altcoins are among the widest here.

security.note: Uphold's security page describes encryption, a Security Operations Centre, regular audits and penetration tests, background-checked staff and a public bug bounty on Intigriti. It does not state what share of customer crypto is held offline.

complaints.note: Uphold Europe Limited is on the FCA's registered cryptoasset firms list (MLRs registered since February 2022). Uphold says its operating entities are licensed or registered in the US, UK, EU and the Bahamas, but no Uphold entity appears in ESMA's interim MiCA register, and no enforcement action was found in this review.

fees.note: Uphold's service fees page (updated 21 September 2026) gives typical trading spreads of 2.05% to 2.2% for BTC and ETH and 2.85% to 3.8% for altcoins in the US, UK and Europe.

transparency.note: Uphold publishes a live reserve status (100.5% when read, with assets and obligations shown in dollars) and says it never lends customer funds unless the customer opts into staking or lending, and is subject to regular US state audits.

products.name: Cash App bitcoin
products.description: Bitcoin-only buying inside Block's Cash App payments app, with free automatic buys and free standard withdrawals to your own wallet. Block has faced large 2025 penalties over fraud handling and anti-money-laundering controls.

security.note: The CFPB's January 2025 order found that 'Block employed weak security protocols for Cash App and put its users at risk' and that its investigations of unauthorized transactions were incomplete. Cash App says it holds bitcoin 1:1 and lets users withdraw to their own wallet at any time.

complaints.note: The CFPB ordered Block to pay up to $120 million in redress and a $55 million penalty in January 2025 over fraud handling. In April 2025 New York DFS separately fined Block $40 million over anti-money-laundering and virtual currency compliance (reported, DFS site not readable here). Block is licensed for virtual currency business by NY DFS.

fees.note: Cash App's bitcoin fee table shows 2.0% on market buys of $1 to $499, 1.5% for $500 to $999, 0.9% for $1,000 to $1,999 and 0% from $2,000, with 0% fee and 0% spread on Auto Invest and Round Ups; quoted fees exclude any spread on market orders.

transparency.note: Cash App says 'We hold your bitcoin 1:1 and never lend it out', but no proof of reserves was published on the pages read. Block files audited accounts as a public company, which do not show bitcoin backing per customer.

products.name: PayPal crypto
products.description: Buying and holding crypto inside a PayPal or Venmo account, run by PayPal Digital, a New York limited purpose trust company, with Paxos as service provider. Convenient but among the most expensive ways to buy here.

security.note: PayPal's crypto terms say some custody, trading and transfer services are performed by Paxos Trust Company and warn in capitals that crypto assets are not insured by the FDIC, SIPC or any other public or private insurer, 'INCLUDING AGAINST CYBER THEFT'.

complaints.note: PayPal's crypto page states that PayPal Digital, Inc. (NMLS ID 2610315) is chartered as a limited purpose trust company by the New York State Department of Financial Services to engage in virtual currency business. No crypto-related enforcement action against PayPal was found in this review.

fees.note: PayPal's consumer fee table (updated 19 May 2026) charges 2.20% on crypto purchases of $1 to $74.99, falling to 1.50% above $1,000, plus a conversion spread, and 1% on crypto sent in one step to an outside wallet.

transparency.note: PayPal's terms explain the Paxos custody arrangement and PYUSD reserve rules, and PayPal Holdings files audited accounts, but no proof of reserves for customers' bitcoin and ether was found.

products.name: eToro
products.description: A Nasdaq-listed social trading platform. In the US it settled SEC charges in 2024 and now offers only bitcoin, bitcoin cash and ether; elsewhere it is MiCA-licensed via Cyprus and FCA-registered.

security.note: eToro's 2025 annual report (Form 20-F) describes cold storage for a significant portion of crypto, multi-party computation (MPC) keys and SOC 2 Type II compliance for custody, but states 'We do not maintain cryptoasset crime insurance'.

complaints.note: eToro USA paid $1.5 million in September 2024 to settle SEC charges of operating an unregistered broker and clearing agency, and limited US crypto trading to three assets. eToro (Europe) Ltd holds a MiCA licence from CySEC (ESMA interim register, 16/01/2025) and ETORO (UK) LIMITED is on the FCA cryptoasset register.

fees.note: eToro's fees page charges a flat 1% per crypto position for most members (lower for high Club tiers), plus market spread, and 2% to move crypto from the platform into its own wallet app.

transparency.note: eToro Group files audited annual reports (Form 20-F) with the SEC as a Nasdaq-listed company; the 2025 report describes segregated omnibus wallets for client crypto. No on-chain proof of reserves was found.

products.name: Bybit
products.description: A large derivatives-focused global exchange with an Austrian MiCA-licensed EU arm. In February 2025 North Korean hackers stole about $1.5 billion in crypto from it, according to the FBI.

security.note: The FBI attributed to North Korea 'the theft of approximately $1.5 billion USD in virtual assets from cryptocurrency exchange, Bybit, on or about February 21, 2025', naming the activity TraderTraitor.

complaints.note: Bybit EU GmbH holds a MiCA licence from Austria's FMA (ESMA interim register, 28/05/2025). No Bybit entity appears on the FCA cryptoasset register, and the global platform is not licensed in the US. No enforcement action was found in this review.

fees.note: Bybit's fee structure (updated 2 September 2026) lists 0.1000% taker and 0.1000% maker for spot at VIP 0, though rates may differ by region.

transparency.note: Bybit publishes a 1:1 proof of reserves with a 23 September 2026 snapshot, Merkle tree self-verification and open-source tools; it is self-published, with an audit report link.

products.name: Fidelity Crypto
products.description: Crypto trading inside a Fidelity account, held by Fidelity Digital Assets, a national trust bank, next to your ordinary investments. A flat 1% fee; no published proof of reserves.

security.note: Fidelity says it secures crypto with 'cold-vaulted storage and secure, monitored facilities' and that custody and trading are provided by Fidelity Digital Assets, National Association, a national trust bank. Crypto is not FDIC insured.

complaints.note: Custody and trading run through FDA, NA, a national trust bank, and FIDELITY DIGITAL ASSETS, LTD is on the FCA cryptoasset register. No crypto enforcement action against Fidelity was found in this review.

fees.note: Fidelity's help page says 'Fidelity Digital Assets ® charges a 1% fee for buy and sell transactions' in Fidelity Crypto accounts and IRAs, which Fidelity says was included in the price as a spread for trades before December 4, 2025.

transparency.note: Fidelity explains who holds the crypto and that it is not FDIC or SIPC protected, but FMR is privately held and no proof of reserves or customer-asset report for Fidelity Crypto was found.

products.name: CoinJar
products.description: An exchange founded in 2013 with UK and Irish arms, a simple app and a low-fee order book. FCA-registered in the UK and MiCA-licensed in Ireland; custody is outsourced to BitGo and Fireblocks.

security.note: CoinJar says its crypto is stored with the custody providers BitGo and Fireblocks, uses multi-level encryption and machine-learning fraud checks, and requires multi-factor authentication for internal systems.

complaints.note: CoinJar Europe Limited holds a MiCA licence from the Central Bank of Ireland (ESMA interim register, 09/12/2025) and CoinJar UK Limited is on the FCA cryptoasset register. No enforcement action was found in this review.

fees.note: CoinJar's UK fees page charges 1% on app conversions and 2% by card, while CoinJar Exchange charges 0.10% taker and 0.10% maker on GBP pairs below £50,000 monthly volume.

transparency.note: CoinJar names its custodians but no proof of reserves or published accounts were found on its UK site.

products.name: Bitpanda
products.description: A Vienna-based investing app for crypto, stocks and metals, MiCA-licensed through several EU regulators and FCA-registered in the UK. Its current fee page could not be read for this review, so fees are not scored.

security.note: Bitpanda says crypto is stored in cold storage facilities examined by an external auditor, and that it holds ISO 27001 certification and a SOC 2 Type 2 report.

complaints.note: ESMA's interim MiCA register lists Bitpanda GmbH (Austria FMA, 09/04/2025), Bitpanda Asset Management GmbH (BaFin) and BP23 CA Limited (Malta MFSA); BITPANDA BROKER UK LTD and Bitpanda Custody Ltd are on the FCA cryptoasset register. No enforcement action was found in this review.

transparency.note: Bitpanda says its funds and business practices are regularly validated by external parties and that it holds 16 European licences and registrations, but no proof of reserves was published on the pages read.

products.name: River
products.description: A US bitcoin-only broker with zero-fee recurring buys, all client bitcoin in multisig cold storage, and a monthly proof of reserves. State-licensed as a money transmitter.

security.note: River says '100% of client bitcoin deposits are kept in cold storage' in multisig, that its custody is not built on third parties, and that it is SOC II compliant.

complaints.note: Indiana's Department of Financial Institutions lists River Financial Inc. with an activated money transmitter licence issued 01/20/2022; River's own page lists state licences from Alabama onward under NMLS ID 1906809. No enforcement action was found in this review.

fees.note: River's help page lists a 1.00% fee on one-time orders up to $1,000,000, falling with size, 0.00% on recurring buys after the first week and on payroll conversions, and says prices may include a spread.

transparency.note: River's proof-of-reserves page shows monthly assets and liabilities, for example 6 October 2026: 33,404.73 BTC of assets against 33,332.42 BTC of client liabilities, with links to verify both sides.

products.name: Spot bitcoin ETF in a brokerage account
products.description: Owning shares of a fund that holds bitcoin, such as iShares Bitcoin Trust (IBIT), through an ordinary brokerage account or pension. You get bitcoin's price swings without handling keys, but you cannot spend or move the coins themselves.

security.note: iShares says the trust simplifies 'the operational and custody complexities of holding bitcoin directly', but still warns of 'the potential for loss, theft, or compromise of private keys' at the trust level.

complaints.note: The trust trades on Nasdaq with an SEC-registered prospectus, but iShares notes it is not an investment company registered under the Investment Company Act of 1940 and so lacks some mutual-fund protections.

fees.note: The iShares Bitcoin Trust page lists a 0.25% sponsor fee per year, with no buy spread beyond the brokerage's normal share-trading costs.

transparency.note: The fund page publishes detailed holdings and analytics, and the prospectus is public.

products.name: Self-custody (hardware or software wallet)
products.description: Buying on an exchange, then moving coins to a wallet whose private keys only you hold, for example a hardware wallet. No exchange can freeze, lend or lose your coins, but if you lose the keys or seed phrase nobody can recover them.

security.note: The SEC's investor bulletin says that with self-custody 'you have sole control over the access to your crypto assets' private keys', and also sole responsibility: if a private key is lost 'you permanently lose access to the crypto assets in your wallet'. Cold wallets are 'generally more secure from cyberthreats' but can be lost, damaged or stolen. Removes exchange failure risk but adds personal loss risk.

products.name: Not holding crypto at all
products.description: The honest floor. The FCA's advice is that anyone buying crypto should be prepared to lose all the money they put in, through price swings, a firm failing, poor segregation of client money or cyberattacks. Not buying avoids all of that, and all the fees.

security.note: The FCA says that if you invest in crypto 'you should be prepared to lose all your money', citing sudden market moves, firm failure, poor segregation of client funds and cyberattacks, and that crypto 'remains high risk with no protections if something goes wrong'. Not holding crypto carries none of these risks.

fees.note: No trading, spread, custody or network fees apply when you do not buy. SIPC also states that it does not protect any digital or crypto asset that does not qualify as a security, so most crypto lacks the protection ordinary US brokerage holdings have.
